# FOOTNOTES AND SCHOLARLY COMMENTARY



[^1]: King Augustus III of Poland (Frederick Augustus II of Saxony, reigned 1734–1763).

[^2]: Sylvester Lubieniecki-Rudnytskyi (Sylwester Rudnycki-Lubieniecki, c. 1708–1777), Basilian Bishop of Lutsk and Ostroh (1750–1777), Exarch of the Metropolitanate of Kyiv, Halych, and all Rus'.

[^3]: Hypatius Bilynskyi (Ipatij Bilyns'kyj, 1704–1771), Protoarchimandrite of the Basilian Order of Saint Basil the Great (OSBM, 1751–1771).

[^4]: The Byzantine Anno Mundi year 7269 corresponds to 1760/1761 AD (September 1 era).

[^5]: The Prophet Nahum (whose name signifies "Comforter" or "Consolation"), seventh of the Twelve Minor Prophets, prophesied the imminent fall and destruction of the Assyrian capital of Nineveh.

[^6]: Slavonic: *пи́вомъ бж҃їя суда̀* (with the potion/drink of divine judgment), a literal rendering of the Greek *τῷ πόματι τῆς θείας δίκης*, referring to Nineveh drinking the cup of God's wrath (cf. Nahum 3:11).

[^7]: The acrostic of the canon in the Greek Menaion is attributed to Saint Theophanes the Branded (Graptos, c. 778–845).

[^8]: Habakkuk 3:13: "Thou wentest forth for the salvation of Thy people, even for salvation with Thine anointed."

[^9]: The Prophet Habakkuk, eighth of the Twelve Minor Prophets, who stood upon his watch (Habakkuk 2:1) and foresaw the coming of God from Theman and the Holy One from the overshadowed mountain (Habakkuk 3:3).

[^10]: Slavonic: *краегране́сїе* (acrostic). The canon bears the acrostic: "Тя̀ проро́че Авваку́ме пою̀ блаже́нне" (I sing of thee, O blessed Prophet Habakkuk), composed by Saint Theophanes.

[^11]: Habakkuk 1:2–3: "O Lord, how long shall I cry, and Thou wilt not hear!"

[^12]: The printed text prescribes *Tone 8, Podoben: "In the highest"* (Въ вы́шнихъ); this melodic incipit in standard liturgical practice refers to the Tone 2 model *Seeking the highest* (Вы́шнихъ и҆щѧ̀ / Τὰ ἄνω ζητῶν) or an abridged reference to Tone 8 models.

[^13]: The Prophet Zephaniah (Sophonias), ninth of the Twelve Minor Prophets, who prophesied during the reign of King Josiah of Judah (cf. Zephaniah 1:1) concerning the Day of the Lord.

[^14]: The Greek acrostic of the canon is: Σοφονίου με φαιδρυνεῖ δόξα. Θεοφάνους (May the glory of Zephaniah brighten me. By Theophanes).

[^15]: Zephaniah 3:14: "Rejoice, O daughter of Zion; cry aloud, O daughter of Jerusalem" (cf. also Zechariah 9:9).

[^16]: Saint Barbara the Great-Martyr of Heliopolis (beheaded c. 306 under Emperor Maximian) and Saint John of Damascus (John Damascene, c. 676–749), Monk of the Lavra of Saint Sabbas the Sanctified, Father and Doctor of the Church, celebrated together on December 4.

[^17]: The Matins canon pairs the Canon of Saint Barbara (composed by Saint John of Damascus, Tone 2, Heirmos: *In the deep of old*) with the Canon of Saint John Damascene (composed by Saint Theophanes the Branded, same Tone and Heirmos).

[^18]: The Church Slavonic reads *ѡ҆фїе́на*, transliterating/adapting the Greek participle *ὀφθεῖσα* (*having appeared* / *seen*).

[^19]: The printed text has *оу҆́є*, an epigraphic misprint for *ѻ҆́ч҃е* (*O father*).

[^20]: Slavonic *є҆диноко́льное пребезꙋ́мїе* refers to Monothelitism (the 'one-will' heresy), while *вѣ́рꙋ же є҆динодѣ́йственнꙋ* refers to the single divine-human operation or Orthodox confession against Monenergism/Monothelitism.

[^21]: The Pochaiv Menaion places the complete All-Night Vigil service for the Holy Great-Martyr Barbara at the end of the volume (following December 31), providing here only the standard Polyeleos/Doxology rank service.

[^22]: Slavonic *зерца́лѡмъ разрѣ́шшымся* (*the mirrors being resolved/abolished*) alludes to 1 Cor. 13:12 (*"For now we see in a mirror, dimly; but then face to face"*), expressing direct beatific contemplation of the Holy Trinity after the dissolution of earthly mortal mirrors.

[^23]: The printed Slavonic has *сообра́въ*, an epigraphic/orthographic variant for *собра́въ* (*having gathered* or *assembled*).

[^24]: Slavonic: *ꙋ҆ꙗзвлѧ́лъ є҆сѝ ꙋ҆́глїе* (literally *thou didst wound/quench the coals*), referring to extinguishing the scorching coals of demonic temptations in the wilderness.

[^25]: Slavonic: *И҆з̾ ꙋ҆лтро́бы ѡ҆ст҃и́лсѧ є҆сѝ*, where *ꙋ҆лтро́бы* is an epigraphic misprint for *ꙋ҆тро́бы* (*from the womb*).

[^26]: Slavonic: *Неꙋдержи́мыми на на́съ сме́рть стремле́ньми и҆тїа̀*, where *и҆тїа̀* is an archaic/epigraphic aorist form from *и҆тѝ* (*came* / *advanced*); the text expresses: *Death came with unrestrainable assaults upon us*.

[^27]: The printed text has *чꙋлодѣ́йствꙋѧй*, an epigraphic misprint for *чꙋдодѣ́йствꙋѧй* (*wonderworking* / *working wonders*).

[^28]: The Slavonic text has *ѡ҆шла́нїемъ слезе́й*, an epigraphic/orthographic variant for *ѡ҆лиѧ́нїемъ* / *ѡ҆мыва́нїемъ* (*by the washing / pouring forth of tears*).

[^29]: The printed text has *Ѡ҆ложи́лъ є҆сѝ*, an epigraphic misprint for *Ѿложи́лъ є҆сѝ* (*thou didst put off* or *renounce*).

[^30]: The printed Slavonic has *ꙋ҆ѻбло́вленнїи*, an epigraphic dittography/misprint for *ꙋ҆ловле́ннїи* (*caught* or *enamored*).

[^31]: Slavonic: *бре́меннꙋю бра́нь* (burdensome warfare/strife); Greek collates to τὴν πάλαι μάχην (the ancient strife/enmity).

[^32]: Slavonic: *Оу҆тро́бъ неѡпа́льнѡ ѡ҆бразꙋ́ютъ*, incipit of the Katavasia of Ode 8 of the Nativity Canon: *The furnace moist with dew typified the image of a wonder surpassing nature; for it burnt not the youths whom it received...* (Ὦδε δὲ τῆς καμίνου δρόσος ἐξεικόνιζε).

[^33]: Slavonic: *ꙋ҆подо́бился сегѡ̀ живоно́снѣй ꙗ҆́кѡ мо́щно бѣ̀ ста́ти*, translating the Greek: κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν τῇ ζωηφόρῳ τούτου στάσει ὡμοιώθης (thou didst become conformed, as far as possible, unto His life-bearing manner of life/standing).

[^34]: Slavonic: *Люби́ти ꙋ҆́бѡ на́мъ*, incipit of the Katavasia of Ode 9 of the Nativity Canon: *It were easier for us to love silence, which is free from danger...* (Στέργειν μὲν ἡμᾶς ὡς ἀκίνδυνον φόβῳ).

[^35]: Slavonic: *сладодохнове́нными* (with sweet-breathing/sweet-blowing). The printed edition has the epigraphic dittography *сладодохонове́нными*.

[^36]: Slavonic: *мгрꙋ̀*, an epigraphic misprint for *мглꙋ̀* (mist/darkness).

[^37]: Slavonic: *невѣ́рное* (literally *faithless*), an epigraphic corruption/misprint for *невѣ́тренное* (calm, windless, storm-free), Greek: ἀχείμαστον λιμένα (a haven free from storms).

[^38]: The liturgical paroemia for Saint Nicholas is a classic composite lection combining Proverbs 10:7, 3:13–16, and 8:4–21.

[^39]: Incipit of the Forefeast Theotokion: *O unwedded Virgin, whence comest thou? Who bare thee, and who is thy mother? How bearest thou in thine arms the Creator?* (Безневѣ́стная дѣ́во, ѿкꙋ́дꙋ прихо́диши).

[^40]: Pericope 36 of the Gospel according to John comprises John 10:9–16, the classical liturgical Gospel lection for holy hierarchs.

[^41]: Slavonic: *Творе́нїе дїофа́ново*, an epigraphic error for *Ѳеофа́ново* (Theophanes the Branded, c. 778–845). The Greek acrostic reads: Σοὶ Νικόλαε θεῖον ἐξᾴδω μέλος. Ποίημα Θεοφάνους ("Unto thee, O Nicholas, do I sing a divine song. Poem of Theophanes").

[^42]: The Greek text of this second canon of Saint Nicholas forms an alphabetical acrostic (ἀλφαβητικός) from Alpha to Omega, with non-acrostic Troika (Trinity hymns) and Theotokia appended to each ode.

[^43]: Slavonic: *стла́мнꙋ* (epigraphic variant for *ста́мнꙋ*, urn/pot), translating the Greek στάμνον, the golden urn holding the manna (Heb. 9:4), a standard Old Testament type of the Mother of God.

[^44]: Slavonic: *побѣ́ды на врагѝ тезоимени́тъ лю́демъ вѣ́рнымъ* (namesake of victory over enemies unto the faithful people), reflecting the Greek hymnographic play on the etymology of Saint Nicholas' name: Νικόλαος, from νίκη (victory) and λαός (people).

[^45]: Slavonic: *бл҃гочести́вомꙋ королю̀ на́шемꙋ* ("our pious King"), referring to King Augustus III of Poland (reigned 1734–1763), under whose royal privilege this 1761 Pochaiv edition was published under the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Contemporary Moscow and St. Petersburg Synodal editions read *правосла́внымъ лю́демъ* or *царю̀ на́шемꙋ*.

[^46]: Patriarch Germanus I of Constantinople (c. 634–733 or 740) composed this festal Theotokion prosomoion (*Вострꙋ́бимъ трꙋбо́ю пѣ́сней*, Greek: *Σαλπίσωμεν ἐν σάλπιγγι ᾀσμάτων*) as a companion hymn to the Doxasticon of Saint Nicholas at the Praises.

[^47]: Pericope 335 of the Epistle to the Hebrews comprises Hebrews 13:17–21 ("Brethren: Obey them that have the rule over you..."), the standard lection for holy hierarchs.

[^48]: Pericope 24 of the Gospel according to Luke comprises Luke 6:17–23 ("At that time, Jesus stood in the plain, and the company of His disciples..."), the classic festal Gospel for holy hierarchs.

[^49]: Refers to Saint Ambrose barring Emperor Theodosius I from entering the cathedral of Milan after the massacre of Thessalonica in A.D. 390, imposing public penance upon the emperor before readmitting him to Holy Communion.

[^50]: The Greek acrostic of the canon composed by Saint Joseph the Hymnographer (c. 816–886) reads: Τὸν μέγαν Ἀμβρόσιον αἰνέσω ("I will praise the great Ambrose").

[^51]: Refers to an incident recorded in the Life of Saint Ambrose by his secretary Paulinus (Vita Ambrosii, ch. 10): a woman in Milan who shamelessly sought to lay hold of the holy bishop and draw him toward her house was suddenly struck dead on the spot.

[^52]: Slavonic: *ѡ҆сти́въ*, an epigraphic typographical error for *ѡ҆ст҃и́въ* (sanctifying).

[^154]: *The Wisdom and Word* (*Премꙋ́дрости* / *Τὴν Σοφίαν καὶ Λόγον*): The printed text abbreviates the Greek and Slavonic incipit to its opening noun in the genitive; the full incipit references the divine Wisdom and Word of the Father.

[^155]: *Conversing privately* (*Бг҃ꙋ ѻ҆со́бь бесѣ́дꙋя*): The printed Slavonic text uses the adverb *ѻ҆со́бь* ('apart', 'in solitude', 'privately'), reflecting monastic solitary prayer.

[^156]: *The firm and God-proclaiming* (*Тве́рдыѧ* / *Τοὺς ἀσφαλεῖς*): The printed text gives the incipit of the Tone 2 Kontakion model, originally composed for the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul (*Тве́рдыѧ и҆ бг҃овѣща́нныѧ проповѣ́датели*).

[^157]: *Psalm-like* (*ѱалѡ́мски водвори́ся*): A direct poetic reference to LXX Psalm 54:8 (MT Psalm 55:7): "Lo, I fled afar off and lodged in the wilderness" (*Сѐ оу҆дали́хсѧ бѣ́гаѧ, и҆ водвори́хсѧ въ пꙋсты́ни*).

[^158]: *Three plants* (*тремѝ сала́тами*): The Slavonic borrows *сала́та* (Greek *σαλάτα* / *λάχανον*), referring to the wild bitter herbs or greens brought by an angel to St. Paul of Latros during his extreme desert fasts.

[^159]: *With the disciples let us go up* (*Со оу҆чени́ки взы́демъ* / *Τοῖς μαθηταῖς συνέλθωμεν*): Tone 2 Exapostilarion model from the Sunday Oktoechos (the second Eothinon Exapostilarion).

[^160]: *O Lord, Thy martyrs* (*Мч҃нцы твоѝ гдⷭи* / *Οἱ μάρτυρές σου Κύριε*): Tone 8 Prosomoion model from the General Menaion for Martyrs.

[^161]: *Acrostic* (*Краегране́сїе*): The Slavonic reproduces the Greek alphabetical acrostic: *Θεόσδοτα μέλπω τοῦ Ἀγγαίου ῥήματα* ('We sing the God-given words of Haggai'), marked as the work of St. Theophanes the Branded (*Ѳеофа́ново*).

[^162]: *Of the divine faith* (*Бж҃твенныѧ вѣ́ры* / *Θείας πίστεως*): Tone 3 Sessional Hymn model.

[^163]: *As one valiant* (*Ꙗ҆́кѡ до́блѧ* / *Ὡς γενναῖον*): Tone 4 Prosomoion model.

[^164]: *Thou hast given a sign* (*Да́лъ є҆сѝ зна́менїе* / *Ἔδωκας σημείωσιν*): Tone 4 Prosomoion model.

[^165]: *By Andrew of Pyrgos* (*А҆ндре́а пѷ́рскагѡ* / *Ἀνδρέου Πυροῦ*): Andrew of Pyrgos (or Jerusalem), a Byzantine hymnographer.

[^166]: *Acrostic* (*Краегране́сїе*): The Slavonic translates the Greek alphabetical acrostic: *Σοφὸν Δανιὴλ ᾄσμασιν στέφω* ("With songs I crown the wise Daniel"), by St. Theophanes the Branded.

[^167]: *Acrostic* (*Краегране́сїе*): The Greek alphabetical acrostic: *Τρεῖς παῖδας μέλπω, καὶ Δανιὴλ τὸν μέγαν* ("I sing the three children, and the great Daniel"), by St. Theophanes the Branded.

[^168]: *Today the Virgin* (*Дв҃а дне́сь* / *Ἡ Παρθένος σήμερον*): Tone 3 Kontakion model composed by St. Romanos the Melodist.

[^169]: *Of Wisdom* (*Премꙋ́дрости* / *Τὴν Σοφίαν*): Tone 8 Sessional Hymn model.

[^170]: *City of ninety walls* (*девѧдесѧтостѣ́нный гра́де*): The printed Slavonic text reads *девѧдесѧтостѣ́нный* ('ninety-walled') rather than *дванадесятостѣ́нный* ('twelve-walled', referring to the twelve foundations and gates of the New Jerusalem in Revelation 21:12-14), a distinctive recensional witness of the 1761 Pochaiv edition.

[^171]: *Not honoring an image made by hands* (*Рꙋкопи́саннагѡ ѻ҆́браза не поче́тше* / *Χειρόγραφον εἰκόνα μὴ σεβασθέντες*): Tone 6 Kontakion of the Three Holy Children.

[^172]: On the prophetic vision of the uncut stone cut from the mountain without hands, see Dan. 2:34–45.

[^173]: Church Slavonic *Мала́хово* represents the Greek ascription *Μαλαξοῦ* ("by Malaxos"), referring to Manuel Malaxos (16th c.), author of several stichera in the Menaion.

[^174]: St. Zoe of Rome (d. ca. 286), wife of the court official Nicostratus, was healed of muteness by St. Sebastian, converted, and thereafter martyred by suffocation over smoke.

[^175]: The acrostic in Greek reads Θεῖόν σοι μάρτυς ἐμφρόνως τιμὴν νέμω ("Divinely do I wisely give honor unto thee, O martyr"), authored by St. Joseph the Hymnographer (ca. 816–886).

[^176]: St. Castulus was an officer of the Roman palace who sheltered Christians; he was tortured and buried alive in a pit on the Via Labicana ca. 286.

[^177]: According to the Passio of St. Sebastian, the twin deacons Sts. Mark and Marcellinus were nailed by their feet to a wooden post and pierced with lances after enduring long imprisonment.

[^178]: The troparion plays on the martyr's name Zoe (Greek *Ζωή*, meaning "life"): "Thou didst attain the blessed life, even as thou wast namesake thereof."

[^179]: December 20 marks the beginning of the Forefeast of the Nativity. Therefore, if the Sunday of the Holy Fathers falls on December 18 or 19 (prior to December 20), the service combines only the Sunday Octoechos with the Holy Fathers, without the Forefeast hymns.

[^180]: For Hebrews pericope 328 (Heb. 11:9–10, 17–23, 32–40) and Matthew pericope 1 (the genealogy of Christ, Matt. 1:1–25), appointed for the Sunday before the Nativity (Sunday of the Holy Fathers).

[^181]: If the Sunday of the Holy Fathers falls on or after December 20 (i.e. from December 20 to 24), it coincides with the Forefeast of the Nativity, and the service combines the Sunday Octoechos, the Forefeast, and the Holy Fathers.

[^182]: The Slavonic rubric *Бѷза́нтїево* reflects the Greek ascription *Βύζαντος* ("by Byzantios" / "of Byzantium"), attributing this sticheron to an early Byzantine hymnographer.

[^184]: Attributed to Cyprian the Hymnographer (9th c.).

[^185]: On the "Angel of Great Counsel" (Greek: Μεγάλης βουλῆς ἄγγελος; Church Slavonic: *Вели́кагѡ совѣ́та а҆́ггелъ*), see Isa. 9:6 (LXX), a prominent Christological title in the hymnography of the Nativity.

[^186]: That is, if the Sunday of the Holy Fathers falls before December 20 (namely on December 18 or 19), this Kontakion and Ikos of the Fathers are chanted; but if it falls on or after December 20, the service enters the Forefeast of the Nativity, and the Kontakion of the Forefeast alternates or is sung according to the Typikon.

[^187]: Cf. Isa. 6:6 (LXX). The live coal (*ꙋ҆́гль*) taken with tongs from the altar by the seraph is a classic patristic and hymnographic type of Christ in the womb of the Virgin Mary.

His relics were translated to Constantinople and laid in the Church of St. John the Baptist in Oxeia, where he became renowned as a healer of hernias and bodily ailments.

[^751]: The three windows commanded by St. Barbara in her father Dioscorus's bathhouse symbolise the threefold illumination of the Holy Trinity, a pivotal episode recounted in her ancient Life and reflected throughout her hymnography.

[^752]: In Ode 5, Troparion 3, the miraculous parting of the rock to shelter St. Barbara from her pursuers is explicitly likened to the deliverance of the Protomartyr Thecla (commemorated September 24).

[^753]: In the Ikos, St. Barbara is invoked as protectress against sudden death and calamities: "па́гꙋбы дꙋшетлѣ́нныѧ" (soul-corrupting pestilence), "гꙋби́телства" (ruin/destruction), "тря́са" (earthquake), and "паде́жа" (pestilence/fatal ruin), reflecting her historic patronage throughout Kyivan and Ruthenian lands as well as the universal Church.

[^754]: In Ode 7, Troparion 4, "въ мѧсосѣ́чницѣ" renders the Greek "ὥσπερ ἐν μακελλείῳ" (as in a butchery/meat-market), highlighting the brutality of the torturers mutilating the holy martyr.

[^755]: Troparion of Ode 8 references Christ's prophecy in the Gospel: "And the brother shall deliver up the brother to death, and the father the child" (Matthew 10:21 / Mark 13:12).

[^756]: Troparion of Ode 9 reiterates the Gospel prophecy of parental betrayal unto martyrdom (Matthew 10:21).

[^771]: Tone 3 Dogmatikon Theotokion conclusion: The phrase "но ѻ҆бо́ю со́бствѡ сво́йство цѣ́ло сохра́ншаго" articulates the Chalcedonian definition of the hypostatic union, affirming that Christ is one Person in two unconfused, unchanged, indivisible, and inseparable natures, each retaining its own distinct properties intact.

[^783]: Headpiece rubric: "Theotokia of the Eight Tones, sung when there is 'Glory...' to the Saint in the Menaion, and 'Both now...' in the Tone of the Saint." In the Ruthenian and Byzantine Typikon, when a saint's commemoration appoints a Doxastikon ("Glory...") at "Lord, I have cried" or Aposticha, the concluding Theotokion ("Both now...") is taken from this weekly cycle of Theotokia in the corresponding Tone.

This hymn reflects the Byzantine and Ruthenian defense of icon veneration defined at the Seventh Ecumenical Council (Nicaea II, 787).

[^848]: Woodcut headpiece and section title: "Resurrectional Dismissal Theotokia of the Eight Tones" (Slavonic: Ѿпꙋсти́телныѧ воскрⷭ҇ны, ѻ҆смѝ гласѡ́въ бг҃оро́дичны). In the Byzantine and Ruthenian rite, these are the Sunday dismissal Troparia/Theotokia (Apolytikia) sung at Vespers, Matins ("God is the Lord"), and Divine Liturgy after the Resurrectional Troparion of each Tone.

[^853]: Tone 5 Resurrectional Dismissal Theotokion: "Rejoice, impassable gate of the Lord! Rejoice, wall and protection of those who run unto thee! [^923]: Photographic documentation of the tail-edge of the closed volume, showing the trimmed, hand-laid rag paper text block secured between blind-tooled calfskin-covered wooden boards of the 1761 Pochaiv Lavra binding.

[^924]: 20th-century archival library shelfmark in pencil ("Стд. 148; інв. 251"), recording its accession in a Ukrainian historic collection (likely the Studite monastic library or National Museum Old Prints collection: "Стародруки" / "Студити", inventory no. 251).

[^925]: Successive parish provenance entries inscribed on the rear flyleaf by Galician clergy, cantors, and parish officers. The earlier faint pencil layers record readings of the codex on November 22 and November 26, 1908, at the Church of Saint Nicholas in the village of Trostianets ("въ Селѣ Тростянци... Церкви св. Николая"), alongside the traditional greeting "Слава Ісусу Христу" ("Glory to Jesus Christ!") and the signature of an assistant priest named Hryhorii ("тої ж Сотрудникъ Григорій"). The prominent ink inscription dated 1941 records the book's custody or transfer to the church committee in nearby Nemyriv (Yavoriv district, Lviv region) under parish custodian Steciak ("1941 Цієй книги / Дану Церкві / Немирові / Комітету / Стеціяку").

[^926]: Exterior of the lower (rear) cover: dark brown full calfskin over heavy bevelled wooden boards with blind-tooled decorative roll fillets, typical of the mid-18th-century monastic bindery of the Holy Dormition Pochaiv Lavra.

[^927]: Affixed paper label in 19th-century cursive ("Простянець.") identifying the volume's provenance from the parish of Prostianets (Trostianets/Prostianets in Galicia). A corresponding cataloguing notation in pencil ("Поз. 3...") appears at the lower corner.

[^928]: Front flyleaf containing a reader's devotional pencil inscription invoking Saint Nicholas of Myra ("Радуйся Николай Великій чудотворец"), patron of the December 6 feast, followed by a cross and the surname Steciak, matching the parish custodian recorded on physical leaf p443. At the bottom is an institutional violet parish stamp reading "ЦЕРКОВА." ("CHURCH.").

[^929]: Archival juxtaposition opening depicting the printed title page of the 1761 Pochaiv December Menaion within its woodcut typographical frame, showing the official state dedication to King Augustus III of Poland-Lithuania (reigned 1734–1763) and ecclesiastical authorization under Bishop Sylvester Lubieniecki-Rudnytskyi (OSBM, Bishop of Lutsk and Ostroh 1752–1777) and Protoarchimandrite Hypatius Bilynskyi (OSBM, in office 1759–1771). The Byzantine Anno Mundi year 7269 corresponds to 1761 AD.

[^930]: Photographic documentation of the head (top) edge of the volume, showing the trimmed rag paper leaves held by preservation foam blocks during archival imaging.

[^931]: Exterior spine of the binding: dark brown calfskin with five raised bands forming six compartments. The second compartment retains its original red morocco lettering label blind-stamped with the title "МИНЕЯ / ДЕКАБРЬ" (Menaion / December).

[^932]: Photographic documentation of the fore-edge (front edge) of the closed volume, showing the trimmed rag paper text block with age-darkened edge toning and surface speckling, secured between the blind-tooled calfskin-covered wooden boards of the 1761 Pochaiv Lavra binding.
